entries.design: cluster-randomized field experiment, 3 arms (control / GPT Base / GPT Tutor), classroom = unit of allocation and of SE clustering; about fifty grade 9-11 classes; four 90-min sessions in Fall 2023; classes assigned to arms 'using an integer program' accounting for scheduling/laptop constraints plus student-count balance constraints (SI A.4); the main text describes the integer program as matching observable characteristics (footnote #); student-to-class assignment by the school is described as random except honors classes (excluded from main sample)
entries.population: high-school students grades 9-11, one large private-sector school in Ankara, Turkey; main sample 839 survey completers (Tutor 277, Control 320, Base 242; SI Table A.1); 943 incl. honors
entries.operation: symbolic_procedure (school mathematics review topics, e.g. combinatorics); exam items 'conceptually very similar' to practice items
entries.intervention: assisted practice phase with GPT-4 chat: GPT Base (standard tutor prompt with the problem) or GPT Tutor (prompt with teacher solutions, common mistakes and instruction to give hints, not answers); laptops supervised by teacher and staff
entries.comparator: business-as-usual practice with textbook and notes; solutions shown only after submission

outcome.measure: teacher-rubric normalized grade 0-1, graded by independent graders blinded to arm (SI A.5); practice (assisted) and exam (closed-book, unassisted)
outcome.assisted: practice phase assisted; primary preregistered outcome = unassisted exam
outcome.delay: none beyond the same 90-min session: exam immediately follows practice; no delayed retention test
outcome.transfer: near: each exam item paired with a conceptually very similar practice item

estimate.metric: ITT regression coefficient on normalized grade 0-1 (Table 1, class-clustered SE); relative % of control mean; preregistered pairwise difference with 95% CI (SI Table A.2)
estimate.value: Exam: GPT Base -0.054 (SE 0.022), GPT Tutor -0.004 (SE 0.013); control mean 0.321, SD 0.277. Practice: Base +0.137 (0.031), Tutor +0.361 (0.032); control mean 0.284. Relative: practice +48% / +127%, exam Base -17% (relative to control mean, NOT percentage points). Preregistered pairwise exam differences: Base vs Control -0.035 [-0.057, -0.012]; Tutor vs Control -0.006 [-0.030, 0.018]; Tutor vs Base +0.028 [0.005, 0.052]
estimate.ci: pairwise CIs as reported in SI Table A.2; Table 1 reports SE only
estimate.k_or_n: 2,848 student-session observations (Table 1); 839 students main sample; about fifty classes
estimate.note: R5 own arithmetic, not reported by authors: Tutor 95% interval from Table 1 approx. -0.004 +/- 1.96*0.013 = [-0.030, 0.021] on the 0-1 scale, i.e. about [-0.11, +0.08] control-SD units (normal approximation, ignores few-cluster small-sample correction). The Base exam effect -0.054 equals about -0.19 control SD. Non-significance of Tutor is NOT equivalence; whether it is non-inferior depends on a margin the study did not prespecify.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Strengths: preregistered primary outcome (unassisted exam), blinded independent grading, ITT, no differential absenteeism (12.3% average), robustness to honors inclusion/controls/clustering (SI B.2). Concerns: allocation is constrained (integer program) rather than a simple concealed random draw, and main text vs SI describe it differently (matching observables vs randomizing under constraints); few clusters (~50 over 3 arms) for class-level allocation; preregistered pairwise t-tests do not appear to cluster SEs; five class-sessions non-compliant; outcome is immediate and near (no delay, no novel transfer); GPT Tutor students could have answers checked during practice; GPT-4 of Fall 2023; single school, school mathematics, Turkey. Mechanism ('crutch') rests on non-preregistered exploratory error-rate and message-cluster analyses. Students' self-perceived learning did not track measured exam performance (SI B.3). Data and code public (GitHub obastani/GenAICanHarmLearning) -> reanalysis possible.

entries.design: two-period crossover RCT in one course; students randomized to two groups (96 / 98) with peer-instruction groups (2-3 students) kept together, i.e. allocation at small-group level; each student had one AI-tutor lesson at home and one in-class active-learning lesson (topics surface tension, fluids); pre-test and post-test per lesson

entries.operation: symbolic_procedure and conceptual physics (first exposure; items 33% analyzing, 41% applying, 21% understanding, 4% remembering per footnote)
entries.intervention: structured GPT-4-0613 tutor ('PS2 Pal') with expert persona prompt and question-specific step-by-step solutions, sequential scaffolding through problem parts, pre-recorded videos, self-paced at home; persona allows confirming answers and giving the answer if the student demands it
entries.comparator: in-class active learning lesson (peer instruction with staff support and instructor feedback) by the course instructors

outcome.measure: post-lesson quiz (not graded; participation credit), written by a separate team member from learning goals; item psychometrics reported in Table S4
outcome.assisted: post-test presumably without tutor; supervision of the AI-condition post-test at home is not described in the sections read
outcome.delay: immediate post-test after each lesson; no delayed test
outcome.transfer: same-lesson learning goals; no separate transfer measure

estimate.metric: standardized regression coefficient for condition (Table S1, student-clustered), plus quantile-regression range in SD units; medians
estimate.value: 0.63 (p < 0.001; R2 0.21); authors' quantile regression 0.73-1.3 SD; median post-score 4.5 (AI, N=142) vs 3.5 (in class, N=174), pre-test median 2.75 (N=316); median AI time on task 49 min vs 60 min assumed in class
estimate.ci: no CI reported for 0.63 in VoR or supplement
estimate.k_or_n: 194 eligible students; medians reported with N=142/174/316 post/pre scores
estimate.note: Internal inconsistency not explained in text read: 194 students x 2 lessons would give 388 post-tests, but medians use N=142 + 174 = 316. Same numbers appear in preprint v1. 0.63 is a covariate-adjusted standardized coefficient, not a raw Cohen d.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Version comparison: core numbers (194/233, 0.63, 0.73-1.3 SD, N 142/174/316, 49 min) identical in v1 and VoR. The VoR adds a 'Context, limitations, and future directions' section (first exposure, Bloom levels, dependence on expert prompts/videos/GPT-4; explicitly no presumption for complex synthesis/higher-order thinking), a note that authors overlap with those who established the in-class approach, FCI/CLASS subgroup statements and a supplement with item psychometrics; v1 headline 'learn more than twice as much' became 'learn significantly more in less time'. Risks: package comparison (medium, location, self-pacing, video, feedback all differ); unsupervised home condition vs class; low-stakes post-test; ceiling effect; no delayed or transfer outcome; exclusion of 39 non-eligible students conditional on completing both conditions; author-developer and instructor roles overlap; no CI for main estimate. Data public (GitHub HarvardAItutor/Study-Data-v4).

claim_edges.locator: VoR Results 'Learning gains: linear regression model'; Supplement Table S1; VoR 'Context, limitations, and future directions' (limitation wording verified in VoR, absent in v1)

entries.bias_and_applicability: Strong design features (preregistration, dual coding, bias-adjusted model) but full text not read: unadjusted estimate, risk-of-bias tool, delay/assistance coding and the ISAR subgroup estimates unverified. Directly relevant population (higher education) and operation (STEM). Key decision relevance: a positive average effect of GenAI in STEM is not robust; activity comparability between arms explains part of large effects.

entries.design: group-randomized trial, Fall 2025; randomization of instructors within 13 blocks of same/similar courses (9 exact-match blocks); ITT with block fixed effects and student covariates, SE clustered by course-section; analysis plan registered on OSF after data collection but before analysis
entries.population: 2,379 undergraduates, 30 instructors, 34 course-sections, large U.S. public university, 11 of 12 schools/colleges; exact-match sample 22 instructors / 1,353 students; 3 non-activating treatment instructors removed from sample
entries.operation: mixed course learning across disciplines (STEM, humanities, social sciences)

entries.comparator: same/similar course sections without the assistant (other AI tools available to all students)

outcome.measure: instructor-posted final grade (0-100) and letter grade (primary); homework score; LMS engagement
outcome.assisted: unknown: researchers did not know which assessments were proctored or AI-permitted
outcome.transfer: course grades, not a designed transfer test

estimate.metric: ITT coefficient in raw points and control-group SD units
estimate.value: exact-match sample with controls: final grade -4.12 points = -0.37 SD; letter grade -0.11 GPA points = -0.13 SD; homework n.s. Full sample: no significant adverse academic effect (text 5.2). LMS total participation about -0.9 SD in both samples. First-generation students: additional -2.87 points (-0.28 SD) in full sample
estimate.note: Only about 15% of treated students ever used the tool (13% exact match); 73.8% of 3,460 requests were direct-answer requests, feedback on own attempt 0.7%. Users and non-users in treated sections had similarly lower grades; IV estimates (-1.99 / -2.83 SD) judged implausible as tool effects by the authors.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Working paper. Few clusters (34 sections, fewer in exact match); adverse academic effect only in the exact-match subsample; analysis plan registered post data collection; student sorting imbalance across instructors; grades are instructor-specific and assessment conditions (proctored/AI use) unknown; survey response 18% with differential response. Internal inconsistencies in the text read: Discussion says a significant difference in the 'full-match' sample whereas 5.2 reports no significant full-sample effect; Discussion cites 7.6% feedback requests whereas 7.3 reports 0.7% (7.6% = navigation). Mechanism (permissive AI climate vs tool use) not identified. Highly relevant as university, multi-discipline, semester-long, naturalistic access condition.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Strong for proximal tutor behaviour and session outcome; distal achievement effect not shown. estimate.value: Immediate post-test: n.s., F(1,205)=0.768, p=0.382. Delayed post-test: erroneous examples > problem solving, F(1,205)=9.896, p=0.002, d=0.62. No condition x grade-level interaction.

entries.design: individually randomised two-group experiment (erroneous examples vs problem solving), six counterbalanced test orders, five sessions
entries.population: 463 sixth graders recruited from two Pittsburgh-area schools; 390 analysed (70 missed a test, 3 removed); attrition not differential by condition
entries.intervention: interactive erroneous examples targeting a designer-specified misconception: find, explain and fix the error; self-explanation prompts; correctness feedback
entries.comparator: supported problem solving of the same problems with explanation prompts and correctness feedback

outcome.delay: immediate post-test and delayed post-test one week later

estimate.metric: ANCOVA on gain scores with pre-test covariate; Cohen d
estimate.value: Immediate gain: erroneous examples vs problem solving marginal, F(1,387)=3.72, p=0.055, d=0.22. Delayed gain: erroneous examples higher, F(1,387)=10.15, p=0.002, d=0.33 (Results, Table 2). No condition x prior-knowledge interaction (median split p=0.55/0.41; continuous beta=-0.04, p=0.36); delayed benefit in both low (d=0.35) and high (d=0.37) prior-knowledge halves. estimate.note: Directly contradicts the prior-knowledge moderation reported by grosse2007errors for this material and age group.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Developer-run; 16% attrition (balanced); effect not significant in one of two schools; near transfer; one-week delay. Learner liking ran opposite to delayed learning, so satisfaction is no proxy. Product consequence: erroneous examples built around misconceptions known from research (not diagnosed per learner) produced a delayed advantage with no evidence of harm for low prior knowledge.
